background.definition: Sarcoidosis is a granulomatous disorder of unknown cause defined by the presence of noncaseating granulomas that may involve multiple organ systems, most commonly the lung, liver, and lymph nodes.

list.listitem: 0.36 per 1000 per year in the United States (black); 0.11 per 1000 per year in the United States (white); and 0.10 to 0.40 per 1000 per year worldwide.
Sweden has the highest incidence of sarcoidosis: 0.64 per 1000 per year.
African Americans: 2.4% in the United States
Whites: 0.85% in the United States
Sarcoidosis is thought to result from exposure of genetically susceptible individuals to unknown antigens.

Proposed etiologic agents include pine tree pollen, clay, aluminum, talc, and various infections such as herpes simplex virus, Epstein-Barr virus, coxsackie B virus, mycobacteria, mycoplasma, and Borrelia burgdorferi.
The disease is more common in women and African Americans, and usually presents in young adulthood.
Granulomas are formed as a result of ongoing inflammation that causes the accumulation of activated T cells and macrophages that then secrete cytokines and tumor necrosis factor-alpha.
Lymph nodes, lungs, liver, spleen, heart, and skin are common sites of sarcoid involvement, although nearly any organ system may be involved.
Consider sarcoidosis in patients with a fever of unknown origin or otherwise unexplained constitutional or respiratory symptoms, especially in high-prevalence ethnic groups. C

Diagnosis rests on a clinical and radiologic picture that is consistent with sarcoidosis, exclusion of other diseases that may present in a similar manner, and pathologic evidence showing noncaseating granuloma formation. B
Diseases that present similarly, such as tuberculosis and histoplasmosis, should be ruled out when considering sarcoidosis. C
A chest x-ray result is abnormal in more than 90% of patients with sarcoidosis. C
Elements of the baseline evaluation include CBC, serum creatinine, serum alkaline phosphatase, serum calcium, ECG, and eye exam. Patients with organ specific symptoms require further evaluation.C

Exposure history, use beryllium lymphocyte proliferation test (BeLPT) to diagnose
Lymphadenopathy prominent, use excisional biopsy to diagnose
Prominent systemic symptoms, urine/serum/bronchoalveolar lavage fluid testing for histoplasmosis antigen

list.listitem: American Thoracic Society diagnostic criteria includes a clinical and radiologic picture consistent with sarcoidosis, exclusion of other diseases that may present in a similar manner, and pathologic evidence showing noncaseating granuloma formation.
Diagnosis of sarcoidosis should be considered in patients with a fever of unknown origin or otherwise unexplained constitutional or respiratory symptoms, especially in high-prevalence ethnic groups.
Pulmonary involvement (dyspnea, dry cough, or chest pain) is noted in more than 90% of patients with sarcoidosis.
Many patients are asymptomatic. Constitutional symptoms (fatigue, weight loss, fever, night sweats, or arthralgias) are found in one third of patients.

Less common manifestations include lymphadenopathy; erythema nodosum; lupus pernio (plaquelike violaceous lesions on the face); uveitis; salivary gland enlargement; and cranial nerve palsies, especially facial. It can also cause an inflammatory cardiomyopathy that results in mitral regurgiation.
Lofgren syndrome is the constellation of fever, erythema nodosum, migratory polyarthralgias, and hilar adenopathy.
A 2020 guideline from the American Thoracic Society recommends baseline eye examination in patients with sarcoidosis to look for ocular disease.

No definitive diagnostic test exists. Diagnosis rests on compatible clinical findings, exclusion of other diseases, and histologic demonstration of noncaseating granulomas. The likelihood of resolution by radiographic stage is shown in Refer to for a suggested initial evaluation.
Chest CT is recommended when there is clinical suspicion for sarcoidosis and may help avoid the need for more invasive procedures.

It is reasonable to begin with endosonography to sample intrathoracic lymph nodes through the airways (endobronchial ultrasound with transbronchial needle aspiration or through the esophagus (transoesophageal endoscopic ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration.

Although a biopsy is recommended, there are a instances in which it may not be necessary for the diagnosis (eg, in the case of Lofgren's syndrome, Heerfordt's syndrome, or a characteristic gallium scan [see below]). A bronchoalveolar lavage with lymphocyte studies yielding a CD4/CD8 ratio of greater than 3.5 provides a diagnosis of sarcoidosis with a specificity of 94%.

Although not found in many patients, particular gallium uptake patterns, when combined with a suggestive CXR, is highly sensitive and specific for the diagnosis of sarcoidosis and may obviate the need for invasive diagnostic testing.
In most patients with a compatible clinical picture (suggestive chest imaging with or without symptoms), a biopsy should be performed, usually transbronchial.

American Thoracic Society guidelines (2020) recommend against lymph node sampling when the clinical suspicion for sarcoidosis is high. They also recommend that in patients with hilar or mediastinal lymphadenopathy, if tissue sampling is necessary then endobronchial ultrasound guided sampling is the preferred sampling procedure instead of mediastinoscopy.

The 2020 ATS guidelines recommend baseline serum creatinine to screen for renal sarcoidosis, alkaline phosphatase to screen for hepatic sarcoidosis, and serum calcium for patients without renal, hepatic, or hypercalcemia symptoms. Vitamin D level is also recommended. All patients should under go CBC and ECG, but the guideline recommends against echocardiogram in patients without cardiac signs or symptoms.

The 2020 ATS guidelines recommend cardiac MRI (or PET if cardiac MRI is not available) for patients with suspected cardiac involvement, and transthoracic echocardiogram if pulmonary hypertension is suspected. If the echocardiogram suggests pulmonary hypertension, right heart catheterization is recommended.

Patients in whom bronchial or transbronchial biopsy is nondiagnostic may undergo surgical lung biopsy if an accessible lesion is identified. However, the finding of mediastinal adenopathy on CT should prompt biopsy by mediastinoscopy before thorascopic or open lung biopsy because it is less expensive and less invasive.

The serum angiotensin converting enzyme (ACE) may be helpful for diagnosis and for monitoring disease progression. In a study in 1035 subjects presenting with uveitis it was 78% sensitive, 90% specific for sarcoidosis (PPV 44%, NPV 97% in this population with an overall prevalence of 11%. LR+ = 7.8, LR - = 0.24).

A systematic review of 8 studies with 649 participants found that cardiac MRI had good accuracy (93% sensitive, 85% specific). However, most studies were small and there was significant heterogeneity. Cardiac PET FDG is recommended when cardiac MRI is inconclusive.
Holter monitoring and echocardiogram is recommended to evaluate for sequelae of cardiac involvement.

For patients without evidence of ocular, renal or hepatic involvement, ATS guidelines (2020) recommend a baseline eye exam, serum creatinine, serum alkaline phosphatase, and optional hepatic transaminases. They also recommend baseline measurement of vitamin D, serum calcium, CBC, and ECG at the time of diagnosis. They also recommend against transthoracic echocardiography or 24 hour ambulatory ECG monitoring in patients without cardiac signs or symptoms.
If cardiac involvement is suspected, cardiac MRI is the preferred initial test, with PET as the alternative if cMRI is not available.

A systematic review identified 6 studies directly comparing cardiac MRI with FDG PET and found that cardiac MRI was more sensitive (95% vs 84%) and similarly specific to FDG PET. The positive and negative ikelihood ratios were 6.3 and 0.06 respectively.

If pulmonary hypertension is suspected, transthoracic echocardiogram is recommended as the initial test. If TTE is consistent with pulmonary hypertension, right heart catheterization is recommended to confirm the diagnosis.
If sarcoidosis is clinically suspected (fever, respiratory symptoms, night sweats), obtain chest imaging. Exclude other diseases, including tuberculosis and fungal infections.
Confirm diagnosis histologically and assess the extent and severity of disease. Biopsy from extrapulmonary sites is usually preferable to bronchoscopy with endofronchial or transbronchial biopsy.
Assess whether the disease is stable or likely to progress, and determine if therapy is necessary based on patient symptoms.
Patients who have mild pulmonary disease and stable or no symptoms should be observed without specific treatment. C

Oral corticosteroids improve chest x-ray appearance, symptom scores and FVC in patients with interstitial lung disease but have unknown effect on disease progression. Methotrexate is a similarly effective alternative.B
Use of other immunosuppressives is reserved for patients with advanced or steroid-refractory disease. C
Patients who have mild disease and stable or no symptoms should be observed without specific treatment.

A recent Cochrane review found that oral corticosteroids improved chest x-ray appearance and symptom scores in patients with interstitial lung disease but had little effect on lung function or disease progression.
Similarly, there is little evidence for the efficacy of inhaled steroids, although inhaled steroids could be considered for symptom relief in patients with cough.

Nonetheless, most physicians feel that progressive, symptomatic disease should be treated, and therapy is clearly indicated for cardiac disease, neurologic disease, eye disease not responding to topical therapy, and hypercalcemia.

Consider oral corticosteroids at an initial dose of 0.5 to 1.0 mg/kg in selected patients with more severe disease. A higher dose (80-100 mg) may be necessary for patients with neurologic or cardiac involvement.
A trial randomized 138 patients with pulmonary sarcoidosis to prednisone or methotrexate. The latter was non-inferior, with both improving FVC to a similar degree.

A systematic review identified 16 studies of which 8 were RCTs of biologics for sarcoidosis. The evidence was most favorable for infliximab but supported tofacitinib for cutaneous disease and efzofitimob in pulmonary sarcoidosis.

A trial randomized 16 patients with sarcoidosis associated pulmonary hypertension to riociguat or placebo. After one year the riociguat group had some improvements in exercise capacity and were less likely to experience clinical worsening.
The evidence is best for methotrexate as a steroid-sparing agent in patients with severe disease and as an alternative to prednisone.

Tumor necrosis factor inhibitors such as infliximab are recommended for patients with persistent disease after treatment with corticosteroids and methotrexate or azothioprine. A randomized trial with 180 patients found modest improvements in pulmonary function.
A phase 2 study of efzofitimod, an immunomodulator that binds neuropilin 2, was found to have a beneficial effect, especially at the 5 mg/kg dose. Further trials are underway.
A phase 2 study found no evidence of benefit for the IL-6 receptor antagonist sarilumab in patients with steroid-dependent sarcoidosis.
There is limited evidence that daily transdermal nicotine patch improves some measures of lung function in patients with active pulmonary sarcoidosis.

A small RCT randomized 29 patients with chronic cutaneous sarcoidosis to an antimycobacterial regimen (levofloxacin, ethambutol, azithromycin, and rifampin for 8 weeks) or matching placebo. At the end of 6 months, lesions had decreased somewhat in size in the treatment group (22-14 mm) but not in the placebo group. Outcome assessors do not appear to have been masked to treatment assignment, though.
AHA guidelines (2025) report no RCTs of treatment of cardiac sarcoidosis. Prednisone 30 to 40 mg/day is initial therapy for symptomatic disease, with the option of adding infliximab or adalimumab.

A retrospective chart review compared outcomes in patients treated with corticosteroids alone (n = 24) or corticosteroids plus either azathioprine, methotrexate, or cyclophosphamide (n = 12). The relapse was 46% with steroids alone and 17% if an immunosuppressing drug was added. This study design is subject to significant bias and confounding, so the results should be interpreted cautiously.
Supplemental oxygen may be necessary in patients with late-stage disease.
In patients with ventricular tachycardia due to cardiac sarcoidosis, catheter ablation may be helpful with acute success in 57% but recurrence in 55%. Procedural complications occurred in 6%.
The duration of treatment will vary from a few weeks to 1 year or longer, depending on the severity of illness and the response to therapy.
Sarcoidosis usually follows an unpredictable course with waxing and waning symptoms. Spontaneous remission occurs in approximately two thirds of patients. B
For patients with pulmonary sarcoidosis, 5 and 10 year mortality were 4% and 9% respectively.
Most patients should initially be followed up every 3 to 6 months. C
Sarcoidosis usually follows an unpredictable course with waxing and waning symptoms.
Spontaneous remissions occur in approximately two thirds of patients.
Fatalities occur as a result of progressive respiratory, CNS, or cardiac involvement.
An Israeli observational study matched 3993 sarcoidosis patients with 19,856 patients without sarcoidosis, and found a significantly increased risk of heart failure (aOR 2.1, 95% CI 1.8 to 2.4).
A systematic review found that hypertension, heart failure, and arrhythmias were common comorbidities in patients with sarcoidosis, but not ischemic heart disease or cerebrovascular disease.
Treatment has not been shown to affect prognosis. It will spontaneously resolve in many patients, especially with Stage I or II disease (see
Negative prognostic indicators include age older than 40 years, lupus pernio, corpulmonale, nephrocalcinosis, and bone involvement.
Lofgren syndrome has repeatedly been found to be associated with a benign course.

In a series of 452 patients with confirmed pulmonary sarcoidosis, and a median age at study entry of 50 years, the 5 and 10 year mortality were 4% and 9% respectively. Risk factors for higher mortality were black race, more advanced disease on CXR, more than 20% fibrosis on high resolution CT scan, or the presence of pulmonary hypertension.

A systematic review found that late left and right ventricular gadolinium enhancement on cardiac MRI and fluorodeoxyglucose uptake at PET both predicted an increased likelihood of major adverse cardiac events in patients with cardiac sarcoidosis.
Staging (I to IV) is based on chest x-ray findings. See for staging and likelihood of spontaneous resolution.
Stage I follow up: initially every 6 months, then annually for at least 5 years.
Stages II, III, and IV follow up: every 3 to 6 months, depending on disease severity and treatment.
Follow-up testing should include a symptom review (dyspnea, cough), physical examination (lung auscultation and skin examination), CXR, and spirometry.

More vigilance is needed in patients with corticosteroid-induced remissions, because of the high relapse rate. In one study, 74% of patients relapsed after achieving a corticosteroid-induced remission versus 8% of patients who had achieved a spontaneous remission.
There are generally no adverse affects during pregnancy.
A flare within 3 to 6 months postpartum is not uncommon.
Diagnosis should be considered in any child who has uveitis, lymphadenopathy, pulmonary abnormalities, and rash.
The distribution of affected organs is similar to that in adults, but the prognosis is more favorable in children.

feature.caption: Suggested Tests in the Diagnosis and Management of Sarcoidosis.
feature.feature_body:
Test Comment
Chest x-ray or chest CT Abnormal findings in >90% of patients with sarcoidosis; used to stage disease
Pulmonary function testing Measure initial lung impairment; establish baseline
Blood count, serum creatinine, serum alkaline phosphatase, serum calcium, vitamin D Rule out infectious etiology; evaluate for organ involvement
ECG Evaluate for cardiac involvement (AV block, arrhythmia)
Tuberculin test Rule out tuberculosis
Ophthalmologic evaluation Rule out ocular involvement, which can be sight-threatening
Brain MRI Evaluate for neurosarcoid; indicated in patients with neurologic symptoms
Cardiac MRI If cardiac involvement is suspected
Serum angiotensin converting enzyme Lacks accuracy as a diagnostic test but may be useful in monitoring disease activity
Endobronchial ultrasound guided sampling If hilar or mediastinal node sampling is indicated
Data from American Thoracic Society guidelines (2020).
